Cytometry in R: A free mini-course for coding beginners.

David Rach1,2, Natarajan Ayithan2, Xiaoxuan Fan2 1 Molecular Microbiology and Immunology Graduate Program, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, USA 2 Flow Cytometry Shared Resource, University of Maryland Greenebaum Comprehensive Cancer Center, Baltimore, USA

As spectral flow cytometry (SFC) panels get larger, the complexity of analysis of cytometry data increases. Unlike conventional flow cytometry and mass cytometry panels, they possess both greater breadth and depth. If analytical goal is to analyze all populations present, unsupervised and semi-supervised methods will need to be implemented. 

Many of these cuttting edge methods are first implemented as free-and-open-source R packages. It is here where new methods tried out, and debates occur. While many cytometry enthusiast express an interest in learning how to carry out analysis in R, they often don't know where to start, especially if at an institution where computational cytometry is not a thing. The resources available often are geared toward users with intermediate bioinformatic skills, forming a substantial barrier to entry. Similarly, not having a place to turn for community support can be isolating when trying to self-study an already unfamiliar topic.

To address this community need, we are currently running a free "Cytometry in R" mini-course, aimed at those with previous cytometry experience but no-to-little coding experience. The course is offered both in-person, and online via a YouTube livestream, with sessions recorded and immediately available. All course materials and code are available via the course GitHub repository. In our commitment to open-science and open-source, these resources are available under copyleft licenses (CC-BY-SA and AGPL3). 

The course was advertised in November and December 2025 on the Cytometry Discord, r/flowcytometry Reddit, LinkedIn and the Purdue list. We received substantial community interest, with over 1500 individuals worldwide completing the interest form. The course started the first week of February, averaging 924 individual participants accessing course resources each week. In addition to the materials, the course runs a Discussion page as a community forum where questions can be asked and topics explored in more depth, providing additional community benefits of being Google Searchable. 

Participant surveys consistently show the course is well received, with both qualitative and quantitative improvement for all learners. All resources will remain freely available upon course completion, forming a permanent contribution and road-map for anyone wishing to learn how to carry out their own analyses in R in the future. Times are changing, while some would rather die than touch a terminal, our course shows that many will if the barriers are breached.
